candidates.story_title: AI assistance enters the Bering Sea pollock assessment review record
candidates.summary_2_sentences: A NOAA Alaska Fisheries Science Center working paper dated September 3rd recommends Model 26.0 for the November and December assessment review. It explicitly discloses AI assistance in document development and model implementation, with authors retaining scientific responsibility.
candidates.why_it_matters_to_alaskans: The eastern Bering Sea pollock assessment informs catch-limit advice; reproducible model changes have direct fishery relevance.

sources.author: James Ianelli; Sophia Wassermann; Carey McGilliard; Grant Adams; Matt Cheng; Cody Szuwalski; Cole Monnahan
sources.fetch_method: Python urllib HTTPS; web search discovered source, direct web open errored

exact_facts: Comparison data cover 1964 to 2024; new 2025 and 2026 observations await quality checks.
47 of 50 dispersed-start fits reached the best solution; all 50 simulated-data self-tests converged.
Separate FT-NIRS age-data comparisons flag lower cohort consistency than traditional microscope ages; consequence remains unresolved.
candidates.quote: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools were used to aid document development and model implementation.
visual_story_fuel: Bering Sea pollock silhouette to otolith rings to scientific review table.
Fifty fit markers: 47 at best solution, three at alternative objective.
Model-comparison plots are embedded in the working paper.
caveats: Recommendation, not adoption or a new catch limit.
AI is documented as authoring/code assistance; Rceattle itself is not established here as an AI predictor.
FT-NIRS is a separate measurement-method issue, not proof of a newly deployed AI system.
candidates.dedupe_status: Not among supplied excluded subjects; confirm run ledger.
candidates.editorial_strength: moderate: strongest clean science lead, but AI role is assisted scientific work rather than autonomous decision-making

candidates.story_title: Koniag's subsidiary is building the automation behind Wingman
candidates.summary_2_sentences: Koniag Government Services said on September 11th that it supports CDAO's Wingman digital-assistant expansion. Its work applies generative AI and robotic process automation to federal workflows including procurement, logistics and financial management.
candidates.why_it_matters_to_alaskans: KGS is a subsidiary of Koniag, the Alaska Native regional corporation with Kodiak Alutiiq roots. This is a named Alaska-owned business building federal AI capabilities; the announcement doesn't quantify Alaska jobs, revenue or shareholder distributions from Wingman.

sources.author: Koniag Government Services
sources.brief_quote: more than $37M in annual cost avoidance
facts: KGS describes support for CDAO Research and Engineering and other defense organizations.
Wingman combines AI, machine learning, LLMs, generative AI, RPA and low-code tools.
The cited cost avoidance belongs to earlier Army procurement automation by a KGS team, not measured Wingman savings.
sources.date_note: Use September 11th, the date on the company-hosted release. The syndicated release is dated September 10th.

facts: KGS identifies itself as Koniag's subsidiary and describes the corporation's Kodiak Alutiiq origins.
The parent corporation lists Koniag Government Services in its own investment portfolio under Government Contracting.
Koniag describes its portfolio as subsidiary companies and its mission as growing earnings and assets to support Alutiiq shareholders and future generations.
Koniag describes its Alutiiq ancestors settling Kodiak Island.

sources.brief_quote: It gives them back nearly an hour each time
sources.quote_speaker: Carin Chapman, KGS VP of AI Strategy and Enablement, quoted by AWS
facts: AWS reports DORA reduced a roughly one-hour contractor-responsibility task to two minutes.
A contracting professional sends a vendor UEI in the email subject; DORA retrieves compliance information through APIs and generates a report for human review and determination.
AWS distinguishes DORA automation from Bedrock-powered Jumpstarter tools that draft contracting documents using LLMs.
AWS reports 687,000 annual labor hours saved and about $37 million annual cost avoidance across Army procurement automation tools. These are portfolio results, not DORA alone or Wingman performance.
AWS connects the prior procurement work to later Wingman work.
sources.limitation: This is a vendor partner case study, not an independent government audit. It has no clear publication date and serves only as background, with AWS attribution on every performance claim.

visual_story_fuel: A UEI enters an email subject, API lookups feed a standardized responsibility report, and a human reviews it. A 60-minute ring contracts to two, explicitly marked AWS case study and earlier Army procurement work.
A physical stack of procurement forms moves through a transparent automation mechanism, with contracting, logistics and finance taking separate paths.
Map Kodiak ownership to federal customer workflows, keeping ownership distinct from local deployment.
Show the earlier Army result as a separately dated evidence card; avoid presenting it as Wingman's measured effect.
candidates.editorial_caution: A fresh company disclosure of support, not a newly awarded contract. No award value, launch date, deployment count or independent performance audit is supplied. AWS is a corroborating vendor primary source, not independent outcome validation. Distinguish non-AI/RPA DORA from LLM-based Jumpstarters. Do not say AI alone produced the entire reported saving.
candidates.confidence: high on attributed company claims; no independent performance verification

Autonomy is verified; this rule does not establish that a specific Alaska team uses machine learning.
